links.targetTitle: The voter-facing Executive Document is reviewed only inside

title: Voters must be able to identify who wrote, reviewed and published an Executive Vote, at entity level and possibly pseudonymously
content:
A.1.10.2.4.8.1.2 says voters should clearly understand three things: "the effects and impacts of the Executive Vote if passed"; "the processes that led to each item being included"; and **"the identities (pseudonymous or entity-level) of those responsible for publishing, writing, and reviewing the Executive Vote."**

Putting authorship alongside content is a claim about how a non-expert actually evaluates a proposal. Most SKY holders cannot independently verify that a parameter change is sound; they can weigh who prepared it and who checked it. Attribution is not decoration around the substance, it is decision-relevant information for exactly the voters least able to audit the substance.

The parenthetical is the interesting concession. Pseudonymous or entity-level identity suffices — no legal names, no jurisdictions. What matters is a *persistent* identity that accumulates a record across cycles, since that is what makes accountability operate. A pseudonym that has crafted fifty Spells carries more usable reputation than a legal name appearing once.

A.1.10.2.4.8.3.6 makes this concrete and even names the parties: the Core Facilitator publishes, while "the Crafters and Reviewers alternate between Dewiz and Sidestream," as determined at the GovOps meeting and recorded in the Executive Sheet. The alternation is itself disclosed, so voters can see that the two teams rotate through crafting and reviewing rather than one team always checking the other.
description: A.1.10.2.4.8.1.2 makes attribution a comprehension requirement alongside effects and process, satisfied by a durable identity rather than a legal one.
